summary: An informational summary of techniques for repairing continuous media streams, like audio and video, that lose packets in transit.

plainLanguage.summary: When some pieces of a video go missing on the way, there are tricks to patch the hole so you barely notice.

subtitle: A survey of ways a sender can protect audio and video streams from lost packets.

tldr.problem: Audio and video streams sent with RTP over UDP lose packets, and the lost packets damage the quality of what the receiver plays.
tldr.mechanism: The memo summarizes four sender-side repair techniques: retransmission, forward error correction (media-independent and media-specific), and interleaving, and says which suit interactive and non-interactive use.
tldr.outcome: It is an informational introduction, not a standard. It recommends low-latency forward error correction for interactive sessions and warns that repair traffic must not worsen congestion.

today: RFC 2354 is an Informational memo from June 1998 and, according to the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It notes itself that it was written before any standard congestion control existed for streamed media.

sections.title: Why Streams Need Repair
sections.content:
Many applications deliver continuous media streams, such as audio and video, using RTP over UDP. Because UDP delivery is unreliable, packet loss lowers the quality of the received stream. Loss repair techniques reduce that damage, and they need differing amounts of protocol support.

The memo calls itself introductory and not comprehensive. It covers only repair techniques that involve the sender of the stream, and leaves receiver-based repair out.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending a live video is like tossing a ball to a friend, and some throws get dropped. This note lists ways to make the game still work when that happens.

sections.title: Units, Packets and Interactive Sessions
sections.content:
A unit is a timed interval of media data from the media coder. A packet holds one or more units. For example, many audio coders work on 20ms units, which are often combined into 40ms or 80ms packets.

The memo assumes the RTP framework: packets carry a sequence number, which shows transmission order and detects losses, and a timestamp, which sets playout order. Most repair schemes send units out of order, so the receiver must schedule playout from the timestamp. A session counts as interactive if end-to-end delay, including coding, network transit and host buffering, is less than 250ms.
sections.plainLanguage: A unit is one tiny slice of sound, and a packet is an envelope with a few slices inside. Numbers on each envelope tell the listener the right order to play them in.

sections.title: How Packets Are Lost
sections.content:
Studies of the Mbone found that in a large conference some receivers will always see loss. Packet traces by Handley showed most receivers losing 2-5% of packets, with a smaller number seeing much higher rates.

Most losses are single packets. Bursts of two or more are around an order of magnitude less frequent, though more common than pure chance would suggest, and bursts of tens of packets are rare. A repair scheme should therefore focus on single losses, try to handle short bursts, and treat large bursts as much less important.
sections.plainLanguage: Mostly, one envelope goes missing here and there, not a whole pile at once. So the best fixes are the ones that patch single missing envelopes.

sections.title: The Four Repair Techniques
sections.content:
Retransmission resends lost packets. It suits non-interactive use but the delay hurts interactive use, and it costs extra bandwidth for the resends and the requests. The memo notes there is no standard protocol framework for requesting retransmission of streaming media.

Media-independent forward error correction (FEC) sends extra parity packets. Basic schemes send k data packets with n-k parity packets so the original data can be rebuilt from any k of the n packets. Parity FEC gives exact repair and light processing, but has higher latency than media-specific schemes. Reed-Solomon codes protect better against bursts but cost more latency and computation.

Media-specific FEC uses knowledge of the codec, for example sending a recoded, smaller duplicate of each unit, which saves bandwidth but gives approximate repair. It adds only a single packet of delay, which suits interactive use.

Interleaving reorders units so neighbours are far apart in the stream. It adds no bandwidth, but it adds latency, so it fits non-interactive use.
sections.plainLanguage: You can ask for a missing piece again, mail a spare, mail a smaller backup copy, or shuffle the pieces so a single loss only makes tiny gaps.

sections.title: Interleaving by Example
sections.content: If units are 5ms long and packets are 20ms (4 units per packet), the first packet could carry units 1, 5, 9, 13, the second units 2, 6, 10, 14, and so on. Losing one packet then leaves several small gaps instead of one large gap, which is often easier to hide, though that depends on the media and codec. The gap size depends on the degree of interleaving and can be made arbitrarily small at the expense of added latency.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of putting a whole sentence in one envelope, you spread its words across several envelopes. Losing one envelope then only drops a few words here and there.

sections.title: Recommendations and Congestion
sections.content:
For non-interactive, broadcast-style streams, interleaving, retransmission or FEC all fit. If approximate repair is acceptable, interleaving is preferred because it adds no bandwidth, and media-independent FEC is next best. In interactive sessions interleaving and retransmission add too much delay, so low-latency FEC is the only suitable repair. For a new codec, media-specific FEC built into the packet format is encouraged; for an existing codec, media-independent FEC is usually easier.

The memo warns that adding large amounts of repair data when loss is detected increases congestion and hence loss. At the time of writing it says there was no standard congestion control for streamed media. As a stopgap yardstick it uses the approximate TCP relation T = (s * c) / (RTT * sqrt(p)), with c in the range 0.9 to 1.5 (1.22 suggested). Its worked example, a DVI audio stream with 204-byte packets, 25 packets per second and a 200 millisecond round trip, gives a loss rate of 6.7%.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending lots of spare envelopes when the road is jammed makes the jam worse. So a program should behave about as politely as a normal download would.
